run_query.title: Run a KQL query
run_query.description:
Execute a Kusto query against a database and return its rows. This is the main tool: everything that reads data goes through it.
Pass values through `parameters` rather than building them into the query text. The query must then declare them on its first line -- `declare query_parameters (state:string); StormEvents | where State == state` with `parameters` of `{"state": "TEXAS"}`. Non-string parameters are given as KQL literals in string form.
Start exploratory queries with a time filter and a `| take`: an unbounded query over a large table scans everything. `server_timeout` is a KQL timespan such as "00:04:00" and caps how long the cluster will spend.
The answer is in `Tables[0]`, as `Columns` and positional `Rows`.
run_query.notes: A query with no time filter can scan an entire table. Bound it before running it on production data.

database.description: The database to query, from list_databases.

query.description: The KQL query. Declare any parameters on the first line with `declare query_parameters (...)`.
query.example: StormEvents | where StartTime > ago(1d) | summarize count() by State | take 10

parameters.description: Values for the query's declared parameters, as a flat map. Non-string values are given as KQL literals in string form.

server_timeout.description: How long the cluster may spend, as a KQL timespan such as "00:04:00".

output.description: The query result, as Kusto's Tables array.

Tables.description: Tables[0] holds the data as Columns and positional Rows; later tables are query statistics.

run_management_command.title: Run a Kusto management command
run_management_command.description:
Execute a dot-command against a database. The general escape hatch for everything the specific tools here do not cover -- `.alter`, `.set`, `.append`, `.create-or-alter function`, policy commands and the rest.
This endpoint can change the cluster. `.show` commands only read, but `.drop`, `.set-or-replace` and `.clear` destroy data, and nothing about the call distinguishes them, so read the command before running it. Prefer the named tools below where one fits, because they say what they do.
run_management_command.notes: The same endpoint runs read-only .show commands and destructive .drop ones. Read the command.

database.description: The database to run the command against.

command.description: The management command, starting with a dot.

output.description: The command's result, as Kusto's Tables array.

list_databases.title: List the cluster's databases
list_databases.description: Every database on the cluster, with its name, persistent storage size, soft-delete period and hot-cache period. The first call against an unfamiliar cluster -- the names here are what every other tool's `database` argument takes.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry DatabaseName, PersistentStorage, Version, IsCurrent, SoftDeletePeriod and HotCachePeriod.

list_tables.title: List the tables in a database
list_tables.description: Every table in a database, with its folder and doc string. Together with get_table_schema this is how to orient yourself before writing a query against data you have not seen.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry TableName, DatabaseName, Folder and DocString.

get_table_schema.title: Get a table's columns and types
get_table_schema.description: One table's column names and KQL types, plus its folder and doc string. Read it before writing a query: Kusto is case-sensitive about column names, and a `datetime` column behaves very differently from a `string` that happens to hold timestamps.
get_table_schema.notes: The table name is interpolated into the command text.

output.description: The table's schema, as a JSON string in the first row.

Tables.description: Tables[0] carries the schema as a JSON document naming each column and its type.

get_table_details.title: Get a table's size and row count
get_table_details.description: Detailed statistics for one table -- total extents, row count, original and compressed size, and the timestamp of the oldest and newest extent. This is the call that tells you whether a query over the whole table is a few megabytes or a few terabytes.
get_table_details.notes: The table name is interpolated into the command text.

output.description: The table's size and extent statistics.

Tables.description: Tables[0] carries TableName, TotalExtents, TotalExtentSize, TotalOriginalSize, TotalRowCount, HotExtents and MinExtentsCreationTime.

list_functions.title: List the stored functions in a database
list_functions.description: Every stored function in a database, with its parameters, body and folder. Functions are how teams package shared KQL, so an unfamiliar name in someone else's query is usually defined here rather than being a builtin.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry Name, Parameters, Body, Folder and DocString.

list_materialized_views.title: List materialized views in a database
list_materialized_views.description: The database's materialized views, with the source table and query behind each and whether it is healthy. A materialized view that is unhealthy or lagging returns stale results without saying so, which makes this worth checking when a dashboard disagrees with the raw table.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry Name, SourceTable, Query, IsHealthy, IsEnabled, LastRun and Lookback.

show_cluster_info.title: Get the cluster's nodes and version
show_cluster_info.description: The cluster's nodes, each with its machine size, state and the Kusto version it runs. Useful for capacity questions and for confirming which cluster you are actually talking to.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry NodeId, Address, Name, StartTime, IsAdmin, MachineTotalMemory and MachineAvailableMemory.

show_running_queries.title: List queries currently running
show_running_queries.description: The queries executing on the cluster right now, with their text, the principal that started them, how long they have been running and the resources they have consumed. This is what to call when the cluster is slow -- the offending query is usually visible here, and cancel_query can stop it.

database.description: The database whose running queries to list.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry ClientActivityId, Text, Database, StartedOn, Duration, State, User and ResourcesUtilization.

cancel_query.title: Cancel a running query
cancel_query.description: Stop a query that is still running, by the `ClientActivityId` show_running_queries reported. The query's caller gets an error rather than a result, so this cuts something off mid-flight -- but a runaway query starving the cluster is usually worth cutting off.
cancel_query.notes: The cancelled query's caller receives an error instead of results.

database.description: The database the query is running against.

output.description: Confirmation that the cancellation was issued.

Tables.description: Tables[0] reports the running query that was cancelled.

show_ingestion_failures.title: List recent ingestion failures
show_ingestion_failures.description: Failed ingestion operations with their error details and timestamps. The first call when data that should be in a table is not: ingestion is asynchronous, so a failed load reports nothing to whatever queued it and only shows up here.

Tables.description: Tables[0] rows carry OperationId, Database, Table, FailedOn, Details, ErrorCode, FailureKind and IngestionSourcePath.

create_table.title: Create a table
create_table.description:
Create a table with a column schema. `.create table` is idempotent only in the sense that it fails if the table exists with a different schema -- it does not drop and recreate.
`columns` is Kusto's own syntax: `Timestamp:datetime, Level:string, Message:string`. Types are KQL types (bool, datetime, dynamic, guid, int, long, real, string, timespan, decimal), not SQL ones.
create_table.notes: The table name and column definition are interpolated into the command text.

database.description: The database to create the table in.

columns.description: Column definitions in Kusto syntax, e.g. "Timestamp:datetime, Level:string, Message:string".

Tables.description: Tables[0] describes the table as created.

drop_table.title: Drop a table
drop_table.description:
Delete a table and every row in it. Irreversible -- there is no soft-delete for a dropped table, and the data is not recoverable from the database's soft-delete period, which governs retention of rows in a surviving table rather than the table itself.
Run get_table_details first if there is any doubt about what is in it.
drop_table.notes: Irreversible. The table name is interpolated into the command text.

table.description: The table to drop, with all its data.

ingest_from_query.title: Append the result of a query into a table
ingest_from_query.description:
Run a KQL query and append its rows into an existing table -- `.append table <T> <| <query>`. This is how aggregations, roll-ups and backfills are materialised inside Kusto without moving data out and back.
The query's output columns must match the target table's schema. This APPENDS: it never replaces, which is the deliberate difference from `.set-or-replace`, a command run_management_command can issue and this tool will not.
ingest_from_query.notes: Appends only. The target table and query are interpolated into the command text.

database.description: The database holding the target table.

table.description: The table to append into. Its schema must match the query's output columns.

query.description: The KQL query whose rows are appended.
query.example: StormEvents | summarize Events = count() by bin(StartTime, 1d), State

Tables.description: Tables[0] describes the resulting extents, with row counts.

ingest_inline.title: Ingest a few rows of CSV directly
ingest_inline.description:
Push a small block of CSV straight into a table with `.ingest inline`. Meant for tens of rows -- test data, a lookup table, a manual correction -- not for bulk loading, which should go through a queued ingestion pipeline or a blob.
The CSV must match the table's column order exactly and carry no header row. Each line becomes one row.
ingest_inline.notes: For small volumes only. The table name and CSV are interpolated into the command text.

csv_rows.description: CSV rows, newline-separated, no header, matching the table's column order.

stream_ingest.title: Stream data into a table
stream_ingest.description:
Push a payload into a table through the streaming ingestion endpoint, which lands data in seconds rather than the minutes a queued ingestion takes. The trade-off is throughput: streaming ingestion is for small, frequent payloads, and the cluster must have it enabled or the call is rejected.
`data` is the raw payload as text in the format `stream_format` names -- newline-delimited JSON for `json`, rows for `csv`. A `mapping_name` referring to an ingestion mapping defined on the table is required for JSON.
stream_ingest.notes: Requires streaming ingestion enabled on the cluster and, for JSON, an ingestion mapping on the table.

data.description: The payload as text -- newline-delimited JSON objects, or CSV rows matching the table's column order.

mapping_name.description: An ingestion mapping defined on the table, mapping payload fields to columns. Required for the JSON formats.

output.description: Empty on success; failures show up in show_ingestion_failures.
